one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens with the recent Turkish jet shootdown of a Russian warplane, which has raised the specter of nuclear holocaust and prompted readers to ask about the aftermath of his two prior WWIII-hotspot columns (May 31 and June 7, 2015). He recalls Gen. Douglas MacArthur's lament at the Japanese surrender: 'War can no longer be controlled. It can only be abolished' -- provoked by the Hiroshima (Aug 6, 1945) and Nagasaki (Aug 8, 1945) bombs that instantly killed over 100,000 civilians and permanently scarred hundreds of thousands more. Despite this warning, several states have accelerated nuclear weapons production via intercontinental missiles, silos, and submarines, raising the prospect of nuclear annihilation in the Middle East, Ukraine, and South China Sea. He paints the cascade: wiping out most living things, searing earth's foliage, melting polar caps, flooding most countries, shrouding the globe in radioactive clouds, ushering in an ice age. He then proposes a 'new world order' he calls the International Peoples Union (iPU) -- a federation of nonindependent nations modeled on the United States, Russia, or Canada but worldwide, with one central government responsible for peace and order for everyone. Unlike the League of Nations and the United Nations, the iPU will not respect state rights but only human rights; its mandate will come not from victors or losers but from victims -- all becoming citizens of one united world rather than separate independent states. It will have an international police force to enforce its laws. A nuclear holocaust has no victors or losers, only victims with one common aspiration: outlawing war and destroying all weapons of mass destruction. First leaders will be self-anointed, organizing survivors in licking their wounds and healing the earth; nuclear energy will propel machines for peace and prosperity. Eventually leaders will be elected worldwide. The iPU will have absolute dominion over earth's resources for the common welfare of all earthlings. In governance, the individual will be supreme; sovereign rights of states will be severely degraded if not totally eliminated. All earthlings will be governed as equal citizens. International law will radically change into the equivalent of domestic law for the entire world. Concretely, the Unclos maritime entitlements -- 12 nautical miles of territorial sea, 200 nautical miles of EEZ, 150 nautical miles of continental shelf -- will become obsolete because there will be no territorial integrity to protect from inter-state incursion. The International Bill of Human Rights -- UDHR, ICCPR, ICESCR -- is currently unenforced worldwide because many states refuse to recognize it, claiming it contravenes their constitutions under the principle of noninterference in domestic affairs. (The Philippines, by contrast, recognizes and enforces these instruments; its SC has accepted them as 'part of the generally accepted principles of international law that are binding on us.') Under the iPU, the Bill could easily be enforced, possibly with modifications to address criticisms that it contains 'Western biases that contradict some religious beliefs.' All peoples of the earth -- regardless of gender, creed, race, language, religion, or color -- will be entitled to equal protection, dignity, and respect. Loyalty will be primarily to the world, only secondarily to nations and villages. Transparency, responsibility, and accountability will be the hallmarks of governance; meritocracy, integrity, probity, and honor will be the inexorable standards for public servants. He closes with the ironic silver lining: a nuclear holocaust may have the unintended consequence of ushering in a new world order making the individual supreme and the state largely irrelevant.
